answers.text: So the rule: three lines, in order — drop-off time, pallet count, and any damage noted ('none noted' if nothing flagged). If the message is missing one, say the time isn't clear, I'd put 'not given' rather than guessing. It stays the same every time because there's always exactly three lines to fill in.
Tell it: list only the calls needing follow-up, one line each — time, customer, topic — then a count at the top that's just the number of lines in that list.

There's a mismatch in the note: access is confirmed from 8am on the 22nd, the crew needs about six hours, so a job starting then would finish early afternoon the same day, not the 23rd as it says. The finishing day is off by one. I'd want that checked before it's filed.

9 late out of 118 is close enough to the 92% written, that bit's fine. But 96 up to 118 works out to around 23%, not the 20% stated. And €29,000 at each region does add to €58,000 correctly, but it's odd to call that 'steady' the same month invoices went up over 20% — worth asking about.

I'd sign off the second one — it gives 940 and 827 and shows the working, so 88% isn't just sitting there on its own. The first is only the percentage; if it were wrong there's nothing in the sentence to catch it. Might be exactly right, it's just not something you can confirm from what's written.

I'd send the second email, the volume numbers and the PO log reference are right there, so anyone can see where 1,200 to 1,650 came from. The first just says 'we'd expect a better rate' without saying based on what, so that claim can't be checked as written. Not wrong necessarily, it would just need the numbers put behind it first.
1. Yes. 2. Yes. 3. No, not signed off. 4. Yes, already public. 5. No, personal address.

The hourly rates and the retainer cap I wouldn't paste straight in, that's the sensitive commercial part. The non-disclosure clause as well, since it names both companies directly — I'd leave that out too.

Before the summary goes out I'd check a handful of the depot totals directly against the warehouse records, not just read the draft over. I'd do that every month, right after the draft's put together and before it goes to finance, picking a few lines to check against source each time. That would catch a wrong total, not just a typo.

Step 4 is where the gate belongs — once the payment note is submitted automatically, it's much harder to unwind than catching it earlier. Step 1 carries risk too, a wrong figure from the PDF runs straight through the match and the note, but it's step 4 where it actually becomes a payment. The gate should hold anything where the match is right at the edge of tolerance, or the extracted total looks unusually high for that supplier.
